data.title: Trump rescinds nearly $1B in federal funding, bypassing congressional approval
data.description:
President Trump cancelled almost $1 billion in federal funding Friday using the controversial “pocket rescission” process, which allows him to sidestep congressional approval.

Most of the cancellations targeted Health and Human Services (HHS) programs serving undocumented immigrants and unaccompanied children in court, as well as similar initiatives under the agency’s Minority Health office and the Department of Education’s Special Programs for Migrant Students.

“These funds previously went to pro-illegal immigration programs and Non-Governmental Organizations that provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens and put unaccompanied children in harm’s way,” the White House wrote in a press release. 

The release continued, “Thanks to President Trump’s successful border policies, the illegal alien invasion is over and there are fewer people crossing our border than ever before.”

The White House went on to say the decrease in border crossings meant funding toward these programs became excessive, warranting their recission

Other cuts aligned with Trump’s anti-DEI agenda — with the president rescinding funds for HHS gender-affirming care research, minority business development and the Department of Justice’s Community Relations Services, which the White House said promoted identity-conscious law enforcement practices. The administration described these initiatives as “wasteful and harmful.”

The president canceled the $810 million in federal funds through a pocket recession, which “occurs when a president asks Congress to rescind (or cancel) funds very close to the end of the fiscal year—so close that the funds expire before they can be used for new obligations,” according to the U.S. Government Accountability Office.

The Impoundment Control Act (ICA) lays out rules governing the rescissions process. It allows the administration to temporarily withhold funding for 45 days while Congress considers the rescissions request. If lawmakers opt not to approve the request, the funds must be released. 

It was last used by Trump in 2025 to unilaterally cut roughly $5 billion in congressionally approved funding. The Supreme Court agreed at the time to allow the Trump administration to keep the money that was set to expire the next week.

data.title: TikTok settles for over $100 million in mental health lawsuit, Alabama AG says
data.description:
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office announced Friday it reached a minimum $100 million settlement deal with TikTok and its parent company, ByteDance, days before a state court was set to hear arguments surrounding the app’s potential mental health effects on minors.

TikTok has 45 days to respond to the settlement, which could balloon to $300 million if certain conditions are met. The move marks the first time the social media platform has settled as it engages in several similar legal battles related to the wellbeing of its minor users, according to Reuters.

In addition to the payment, the agreement also requires that TikTok implement a host of safety features designed to protect children using its platform — including daily time limits, stronger content moderation, more user-friendly parental controls and a blanket prohibition on cosmetic filters by teen users.

It also mandates that the app add “productive pauses” that interrupt teen users after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use “to limit endless scrolling.”

The app will also add nighttime restrictions as a result of the settlement, restricting children’s access to TikTok from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m. and placing blocks on notifications during this period. The settlement says the platform must add similar restrictions during school hours.

Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall’s office accused the company last year of making its platform purposefully addictive for young users and negatively impacted the wellbeing of teenagers in the state. 

TikTok has defended itself in the past by saying it designed the platform with teen safety in mind, which a federal judge ruled against. 

“This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app,” Marshall wrote in a press release about the settlement deal. 

When asked about the settlement, a TikTok U.S. Data Security Joint Venture spokesperson told The Hill, “TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community.”

“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson continued.

data.title: Francesca Hong says she regrets CNN interview about Thanksgiving
data.description:
Francesca Hong, a former democratic socialist candidate in the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, said Friday she regrets her controversial CNN interview where she stated she wanted to “cancel Thanksgiving.”

In an interview with WISN, a local ABC affiliate, anchor Matt Smith reflected on Hong’s time on the campaign trail and asked if there was anything she would have done differently in the lead up to Wisconsin’s gubernatorial primaries in August.

“I was never going to cancel Thanksgiving. Actually, love to celebrate the holidays,” Hong said. 

Ahead of the state’s Democratic primary, Hong’s past social media posts where she called for an end to Thanksgiving, where she stated that it “should have done this in 1621,” resurfaced. Backlash surrounding the democratic socialist grew when she defended her comments during a CNN interview in the week leading up to the primaries.

“I think there I wanted to make sure that people understood that there are multiple views, but views can evolve,” she said at the time.

Days later, in an interview with Politico, Hong walked back her take on Thanksgiving — telling the outlet she “actually loves” the holiday. Around the same time, she told The Hill that her original comments “could” have been made in jest.

When asked if she regretted the CNN interview and if she saw it as defining moment for her campaign in the lead up to the primaries, Hong responded, “It was a regrettable moment.”

“And I do regret that interview,” she concluded. 

Hong added that she wished she would have leaned further into her Wisconsin roots during the campaign trail.

“I’m a daughter of Wisconsin, born and raised in this state. There’s nothing I love more than Packer games, Culvers and making sure that my community has the things that they need,” she said.

“We needed to reach more people with that message,” Hong added. “I’m incredibly proud of the movement that we built, the enthusiasm that is still there.”

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly beat Hong in be the Democratic candidate in the race to replace retiring Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers (D). Despite polling from July placing Hong nearly 25 points ahead of Crowley, she lost to him by more than 3,000 votes when the race was called by Decision Desk HQ.

The loss marked a significant hit to the growing democratic socialist movement and gave moderate Democrats a much-needed boost ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

data.title: White House defends pro-Trump TV ads timed with midterms: 'Patriotism isn't partisan'
data.description:
The White House defended the pro-President Trump television campaign that aired this week ahead of the 2026 midterm election, saying, “patriotism isn’t partisan.”

“The announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad,” the White House wrote in a press release. “These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country — not a line on the ballot.”

The 30-second commercial features Trump’s voice, saying, “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and “America will never be a communist country.” The song “Love Me” by JMSN, whose name is Christian Berishaj, plays in the background.

The ad used 2024 remarks from UFC President Dana White, describing the president as “the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met and nothing is going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country that he’s lost.”

The ad’s disclaimer reads, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The White House cited multiple examples of presidents in the past using similar ad campaigns “to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction.”

The list included former President Biden’s “We can do this” vaccine commercials from 2021 that encouraged Americans to get vaccinated against COVID during the pandemic. 

It also stated that “the announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action.”

Trump has endorsed a number of candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, and in August, encouraged voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

He invoked this same messaging tactic during a rally for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) for her runoff election in the Palmetto State.

AdImpact, a political media monitoring company, estimated the Trump administration spent more than $400,000 to run the ads, according to the Associated Press. The outlet also reported that the ad is running on primetime and morning shows on CBS and various Fox News programming.

AdImpact wrote on social media that Trump’s July 4th advertisement began airing Friday. It featured Trump narrating alongside a montage of pictures of the president delivering remarks at Mount Rushmore.

data.title: Iran pitches 7-day plan to restart US talks, reopen Strait of Hormuz
data.description:
Iran has shared a seven-day plan with the U.S. to end fighting between the two countries,  reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks for a final peace deal, Tehran’s foreign minister told multiple outlets Thursday in New York City.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a group of reporters at the UN General Assembly that “if certain conditions are met” by Washington, the strait would be opened at the end of the plan’s seven days.

Araghchi noted that the terms of the proposal, given to the U.S. through intermediators, closely matched commitments in the now dead 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed by Washington and Tehran in June. That deal unraveled amid renewed fighting in July.

With a seven-day timeline, the new deal would move at a much faster pace than the MOU, which had a 60-day time frame for restarting nuclear talks.

Araghchi said Iran was ready to start the plan as soon as the Trump administration agreed to it, and that “it would be better,” if a deal was reached before the November midterm elections.

A U.S. official told The New York Times that the administration was having constructive talks through mediators but was not going to rush into any agreement.

The Iranian plan comes after Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that his country is willing to strike a deal with the U.S. before the midterms, pushing back on President Trump’s claim that the regime is waiting until after Americans hit the polls to settle the conflict.  

Trump and Pezeshkian delivered fiery speeches at the UN General Assembly earlier this week, during which, the U.S. president threatened Iran with “annihilation” if it did not make a deal. Pezeshkian, in turn, said Iran would not be bullied.

Araghchi said the latest proposal would end all hostilities in Iran and Lebanon during the seven days; Washington would release billions of dollars in Tehran’s frozen assets, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade on Iran; and only on the last day would the Strait of Hormuz be reopened, as reported by the Times.

Following the seven days, the two sides would immediately begin comprehensive negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program.

Trump has reportedly been frustrated by a lack of onramp to the Iran war, which has stretched on for nearly seven months after the president initially insisted the conflict would only take a matter of weeks.

The deeply unpopular conflict has crippled the global energy market due to the closure of the strait, causing energy and food prices to spike.

data.title: Supreme Court blocks use of GOP-favored map in Missouri — again
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday blocked a directive for Missouri Republicans to use their favored congressional map, making clear to officials they must return to an old design for November after the state’s messy redistricting battle. 

The decision is a blow for the GOP, which fought to use a more favorable 7-1 House map in time for the November midterms instead of the older 6-2 map.

Republicans had passed their 7-1 congressional lines last year and used it during their August primaries, but the high court’s decision means the Show Me State will now be using a different set of maps for the general election. 

“In short, as a matter of state law, the 2022 map—not the2025 map—must be used in the 2026 congressional election,” the court wrote in its unsigned opinion. 

There were no noted dissents. 

It’s the third time the battle reached the Supreme Court in as many weeks. In each round, the GOP has lost. 

The Show Me State has been roiled by several different lawsuits regarding Republicans’ new 7-1 House map, which was created amid pressure from President Trump and national Republicans as the GOP has sought to add pickup opportunities to the lower chamber ahead of the fall.  

Republicans sought to dismantle Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based district. But Cleaver appears poised to win reelection with the state reverting back to using its old lines. 

The legal battle plunged into chaos earlier this month when Missouri’s top court ruled that a referendum over the congressional lines will now go before voters, meaning that the new 7-1 House map does not go into effect until it’s passed.  

By that point, Missouri had already used the design to select primary winners. Several GOP congressional candidates began convincing a federal judge that reverting so late to the old map would be unconstitutional. 

This Supreme Court previously lifted the judge’s order, appearing to signal that Republicans wouldn’t be able to redistrict in time for November. But that didn’t stop the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. On Monday, it issued a new ruling effectively reinstating the state’s 7-1 map. It was set to take effect next week. 

That’s what led to the latest round at the Supreme Court. The referendum organizer fighting the GOP brought the new ruling back to the justices, seeking an emergency intervention. 
 
“This case is back before this Court for a familiar reason: a lower court has once again granted relief this Court foreclosed,” the organizer’s attorneys wrote in court filings. 
 
He emphasized that election officials had already started mailing out military and overseas ballots on Saturday using the 6-2 House map. The Supreme Court’s decision allows election officials to proceed as usual, with no need to make last-minute changes to their ballots before the general.  

However, the late litigation is frustrating for candidates and voters. Election officials and contenders are racing to educate voters about who’s on their ballot and which congressional district they’re in with just weeks out from the election. 

Politically, the Supreme Court’s decision has little impact on the national redistricting math as Republicans had only sought to add one pickup opportunity to their column in Missouri.

data.title: Democratic senators accuse Kennedy of not adhering to ethics agreement in vaccine lawsuit
data.description:
A group of Senate Democrats questioned whether Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. potentially concealed an agreement to collect money from a settlement with a vaccine manufacturer despite pledging to divest from the lawsuit.

At the time of his confirmation process last year, Kennedy was still involved in a lawsuit carried out by the law firm Wisner Baum against Merck over its HPV vaccine Gardasil, alleging that it caused neurological and autoimmune injuries.

Merck agreed to pay $50 million earlier this year to settle the lawsuit without admitting any guilt, maintaining its product was safe and effective. Wisner Baum confirmed soon after that neither Kennedy nor his son would receive from the settlement, contradicting what the secretary told Congress about how he would handle his divestment.

The discrepancy drew skepticism from Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.), Ron Wyden (Oreg.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and Angela Alsobrooks (Md.).

“It is possible you made this valuable concession expecting nothing in return. But if the agreement involves any kind of implicit or explicit agreement with Wisner Baum about future payments or other future rewards in exchange for your Gardasil stake, it would prompt concerns about your ongoing conflicts of interest with the firm, and about the integrity of your decisions at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS),” they wrote in a letter to Kennedy.

While Kennedy at first indicated his plans to retain part of the fees awarded in the case, arguing at the time that he was “entitled” to that money and wasn’t actively involved in the case as an attorney, he later committed to divesting his interest and instead assigning them to his son.

Kennedy’s son, Conor Kennedy, is an associate at Wisner Baum, though he is not listed among counsel involved with the Gardasil case. In an August letter to Warren, HHS Assistant Secretary for Legislation Gary Andres confirmed the health secretary had irrevocably assigned his interests in the case to Wisner Baum.

“The modification also raises questions about the conditions and circumstances under which you decided to relinquish the stakes back to Wisner Baum. You have provided no explanation for this change, and you have failed to clarify whether it may entitle you to additional benefits or other considerations from Wisner Baum upon leaving government,” the lawmakers added.

“If you made any kind of implicit or explicit agreement for future payment or other future rewards with Wisner Baum in exchange for assigning them this stake, it would mean that you have an ongoing conflict of interest that calls into question your integrity and the motivations for your decisions as HHS Secretary.”

The Hill has reached out to HHS for comment.
